assumptions: Arrival context: Layla's assistant found the post while looking at options for her mother's 60th, to be held the year after the wedding with family flying in from Dubai, Sydney and London. The assistant reads first and summarises for Layla.
HTML comments, image slot notes and fact markers are invisible to this reader.

Business details (fees, commissions, on the ground support, transfers, room blocks, Wedded Privileges, phone lines) are deliberately deferred, so I have not marked them down or suggested edits for them.

checks.check: Every journey point, turn-off and CTA reaction quotes an exact sentence or phrase from the draft
Stayed in character as Layla (UHNW, Dubai, assistant reads first, judges in seconds)
No invented brand facts; anything the page does not say is listed as an unanswered question
Every suggested edit 'old' is an exact, unique substring of 05-draft.md
No suggested edit adds prices, fees, commissions, vendor names, statistics, em dashes or deferred business details
Australian English, no em dashes in this file

open_questions.question: This post reads as a general how-to for a home party or a small weekend away. Is the UHNW persona meant to be a target reader here, or should my low relevance score be weighted down for this topic?

first_impression.reaction: The opening is calm and doesn't try too hard, which I like. "The celebrations that land well start with the guest of honour" is sensible. But nothing on the first screen tells me this is for a family like mine. My assistant would keep going only to see if there's anything on scale or privacy, and would skim most of the practical lists.

journey.quote: Who do they want in the room, how do they like to spend an evening, and would they rather be fussed over at home or taken somewhere new?
journey.reaction: Fine. Understated, no hype. It doesn't sound like a package sale, which matters to me.

journey.quote: A draught can melt wax unevenly and tip a candle over, so on a terrace or near an open door, battery candles are a safe alternative.
journey.reaction: I don't need to be told about candle safety. Battery candles at my mother's 60th? This is written for someone doing it themselves. My assistant would skip it.

journey.section: A long lunch or garden party
journey.quote: Leave SPF50+ sunscreen and hats at the entrance.
journey.reaction: Sensible for Australia, but it's over-explaining. It makes the whole thing feel like a backyard party guide.

journey.quote: A long weekend with close friends at a villa or a small hotel: one anchor dinner, a long lunch, and the rest left open.
journey.reaction: Nice tone, but it assumes a small group. Nothing here suggests anyone has thought about 150 family members flying in.

journey.quote: Plan for comfort first: short journeys, rooms without stairs where needed, and one evening when everyone sits down together.
journey.reaction: This is the closest to us. Thoughtful about the older relatives. I'd want one line that shows awareness of family customs and food rules, without making assumptions.

journey.section: Choose the date and book the anchor event
journey.quote: Is it exclusive use, or are spaces shared with other guests?
journey.reaction: Good, the right question. This is the first moment it sounds like someone who knows what matters. I'd go further: can the whole property be closed.

journey.section: Settle the guest list and your priorities
journey.quote: Decide early who pays for what, such as hosting the dinner while guests cover their flights, and say so plainly in the invitation.
journey.reaction: Not our world, we host everything. Not offensive, just tells me I'm not the reader.

journey.quote: Declare everything upfront, including pre-existing health conditions, or the policy may be void.
journey.reaction: Correct, I'm sure, but it's a lot of admin for a planning article. My assistant would scroll straight past this block.

journey.section: Where everyone stays and one hosted dinner
journey.quote: one Wedded Advisor, start to finish, as a single point of contact, working in your time zone and quoting in AUD for Australian couples.
journey.reaction: A single point of contact is what I want. But 'for Australian couples' on a birthday post feels like a standard client line, and we're split across three countries.

journey.section: Planning a milestone birthday for someone else
journey.quote: For a surprise, say clearly what must stay secret and keep it off social media.
journey.reaction: The only mention of keeping things private, and it's only about surprises. For us, privacy isn't about the surprise, it's the default.

journey.section: Planning a milestone birthday with Wedded Concierge
journey.quote: One Wedded Advisor plans the venue, travel, vendors and payments with you, anywhere in the world, and the fee is agreed in writing before any work begins.
journey.reaction: Clean and calm. 'Anywhere in the world' and 'agreed in writing' are reassuring. It doesn't beg. Still nothing about scale or discretion.

unanswered_questions: Has Wedded Concierge planned a celebration for 200 or more guests, and travelling from several countries?
How is discretion handled: confidentiality for the family, guest lists and photos?
Can a planner work with our own security team and the venue's?
Can the Wedded Advisor work with my assistant or the family office as the day-to-day contact?
Is a first conversation kept confidential before we commit to anything?

turn_offs_found.quote: battery candles are a safe alternative
turn_offs_found.why: Over-explaining. Reads like a DIY guide, not someone who handles events at our level.

turn_offs_found.quote: quoting in AUD for Australian couples
turn_offs_found.why: Feels like a standard client line, and 'couples' is the wrong word on a birthday post.

turn_offs_found.quote: A long weekend with close friends at a villa or a small hotel
turn_offs_found.why: Assumes small scale. No hint that taking a whole property is an option.

would_share_with: My assistant would summarise the venue questions and the multi-generation section for my mother's 60th, nothing more.

cta_reaction.why: The wording is understated and I like 'start a conversation' more than 'book now'. But I enquire through referrals or a private channel, and nothing here shows they've handled our scale or care about privacy. My assistant might click to look, not to enquire.

top_3_changes: Treat privacy as normal, not just a surprise tactic: one line advising hosts to set a no-sharing rule with guests, the venue and suppliers.
Show that scale is possible: mention taking a whole property for the weekend, and add a venue question about closing it to the public.
Drop 'for Australian couples' from the Wedded Advisor line; families plan across countries and this is a birthday, not a wedding.

suggested_edits.old: For a surprise, say clearly what must stay secret and keep it off social media.
suggested_edits.new: For a surprise, say clearly what must stay secret and keep it off social media. Even without a surprise, some families prefer that nothing is shared at all; say so in the invitation and ask the venue and suppliers to agree to the same.
suggested_edits.reason: Privacy is the default for families like mine, not only a surprise tactic. One sentence signals discretion without over-explaining.

suggested_edits.old: - Is it exclusive use, or are spaces shared with other guests?
suggested_edits.new: - Is it exclusive use, or are spaces shared with other guests? Can the whole property be closed to the public for your stay?
suggested_edits.reason: Exclusive use is the first thing I'd ask. Going one step further shows the writer understands larger, private celebrations.

suggested_edits.old: A long weekend with close friends at a villa or a small hotel
suggested_edits.new: A long weekend with close friends at a villa, a small hotel or a whole property taken for the weekend
suggested_edits.reason: The section assumes small scale. Mentioning a whole property keeps the tone and quietly widens who it speaks to.

suggested_edits.old: and one evening when everyone sits down together.
suggested_edits.new: and one evening when everyone sits down together. Ask the family early about customs, food requirements and timings that matter to them, so the menu and the schedule fit.
suggested_edits.reason: Multi-generation family celebrations often carry customs. Asking, rather than assuming, shows cultural awareness without stereotyping.

suggested_edits.old: quoting in AUD for Australian couples
suggested_edits.reason: 'Couples' is the wrong word on a birthday post, and 'Australian' makes families based overseas feel like they're not the client.
